[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.


[Information Sparsity]
You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.


[Cognitive Load]
Cumulative cognitive load so far in this discussion -- the raw sum of your per-turn 1-5
workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5; higher = more worn down):
8.5
This turn's workload breakdown (from your own NASA-TLX self-report just now):
mental_demand=1.0, performance=1.0, effort=1.0, frustration=1.0 (overall=1.0/5). Dominant driver: mental_demand.


[Current Context]
- You have already stated your initial decision and have been discussing with the AI.
- Form your judgment based on the conversation so far, filtered through your persona
  above -- it governs how readily you should update "belief" below.

[Task]
Respond to the AI partner's latest message.
- You may maintain your previous position, update it based on the AI's reasoning,
  or refine your view.
- Be clinically plausible and grounded in the case facts.
- Do NOT invent new findings not present in the case description.

[Termination Decision]
Decide CONTINUE or END. Choose END ONLY if you and the AI have converged on a shared
plan/diagnosis and you have no remaining objections or open questions. Otherwise CONTINUE.

[Style Constraint]
- Keep your response under 5 sentences.
- Focus on clinical evidence.

"argument_validity" first, then let it inform "belief" -- do not decide belief first and

{

Case:
A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

case_info.caption: Transthoracic echocardiogram with apical 4-chamber views showing severe mitral regurgitation at a heart rate of 95 beats per minute (bpm), with wide QRS on monitoring (A), and minimal mitral regurgitation at a resting heart rate of 58 bpm, with narrow QRS on monitoring (B).
case_info.explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. case_info.explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).
